newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RBNZ comment won't dim appetite for NZ - analysts.
newsitem.headline: RBNZ comment won't dim appetite for NZ - analysts.

text.p: Foreign investors' appetite for New Zealand assets is unlikely to be dimmed by a Reserve Bank of New Zealand statement on Thursday endorsing lower interest rates and a lower Kiwi dollar, analysts said.
While the pace of eurokiwi and samurai bond issuance might ease up, New Zealand's yields even at new lower levels were still too tempting for offshore investors to resist, they said.

"New Zealand interest rates, even at nine percent, are still relatively high compared with those in Japan and Europe, although the pace of issues may slow in coming weeks," Macquarie Bank economist Joanne Gudgin told Reuters Financial Television.
The New Zealand dollar plunged by three quarters of a U.S. cent and 90-day bank bills lost 34 basis points after the RBNZ said the recent firming of monetary conditions had gone too far.
Just a week before, the central bank had sent the kiwi dollar spiralling upwards when it said there was no room for a monetary easing despite lower-than-expected inflation data.
"I think the signs were out there for an easing. It just came in a little sooner than the market had anticipated," the Sydney-based Gudgin told RFTV.
"As interest rates come off, we would expect the New Zealand dollar to come off a little bit further," she said.
However, analysts said barring a significant fall in interest rates, the currency was unlikely to decline much further.

"If the short-term interest rates remain above nine percent, I expect good support for the Kiwi around the 69.75 cent level," Oliver Kam, assistant director of Standard Chartered Asia in Hong Kong, told RFTV.
Graham Bibby, managing director of Richmond Asset Management in Hong Kong, said the market had over-reacted to the bank's statement and should find solid support around 69.70 cents.
"As long as that support level holds, I think foreign investors will be moving back into the Kiwi," he told RFTV.
The bank's statement came as New Zealand's political parties continue negotiations on forming a coalition government in the wake of an inconclusive general election on October 12.
Macquarie Bank's Gudgin said the RBNZ, in framing its statement, was unlikely to have had any insight into the likely outcome of the negotiations.
"However, the comments may suggest they are a little bit less concerned about fiscal slippage going into 1997," she said.
